articles.full_text:
US yields are falling, Fed tightening expectations are easing, yet the dollar remains firm. French debt concerns may help explain why, with several major currency pairs approaching important technical levels.
- DXY's relationship with front-end yields abruptly turns negative
- Euro weakness offsets retreat in Fed tightening expectations
- US CPI backtesting reveals no consistent directional trading advantage
- DXY, EUR/USD and USD/JPY test important technical levels
US dollar resilience faces a busy week
The US dollar enters a busy week for economic data, headlined by CPI, PPI and retail sales on Wednesday and Thursday. However, while those releases will be the headline acts, what may be of greater interest is the abrupt breakdown in the dollar's relationship with front-end US Treasury yields.
Having maintained a generally positive relationship through much of this year, correlations have deteriorated sharply in October, with the dollar continuing to strengthen despite a partial reversal of September's surge in US yields and reduced expectations for further Fed tightening. Without renewed concerns over France's public finances weighing heavily on the euro, it's possible the dollar would already be trading considerably lower.
DXY's relationship with US Treasury yields breaks down
You can see the deterioration in the dollar's relationship with front-end US Treasury yields in the graphic below. As recently as the end of September, the 10-session rolling correlation between DXY and US two-year yields stood at +0.66, with the 20-session measure at +0.55. By the end of last week, those readings had fallen to −0.39 and +0.19, respectively.
Source: LSEG
Similar movements have been seen against five-year yields in the belly of the curve, suggesting the change isn't confined to just the front end. Since the end of September, DXY has risen around 0.75%, despite US two-year yields falling 9.6 basis points and five-year yields declining 6.8 basis points over the same period.
Fed pricing retreats, but the dollar holds firm
Following the softer US payrolls report earlier this month, along with what appears to have been a concerted effort by Fed officials to push back against expectations for another rate hike in October, markets have reduced their expectations for further tightening. As shown in the graphic below, cumulative tightening priced through the end of next year has fallen from just over 100 basis points in mid-September to around 80 basis points.
Source: TradingView
Had the dollar maintained the positive relationship with front-end Treasury yields seen earlier this year, it suggests that, all else being equal, the greenback would be weaker than where it is today.
However, currencies don't trade on US developments alone. Renewed concerns over France's public finances, fears of spillovers into other European debt markets and higher energy prices have weighed heavily on the euro. Given its 57.6% weighting in DXY, that weakness may explain why the dollar has remained so resilient despite the retreat in US rate expectations.
CPI brings volatility, but little directional certainty
While there's plenty of important US economic data coming our way this week, historical patterns offer little guidance on directional risks for the dollar. Backtesting of 188 CPI releases since 2011 shows that although the dollar tends to experience larger moves on inflation reporting days, there's little evidence of a consistent tendency to either extend or reverse its prevailing trend.
That suggests traders should keep a close eye not only on the incoming US data, but also on developments in European debt markets, which may prove just as influential in determining where the dollar heads next.
DXY: Bullish continuation pattern takes shape
Source: TradingView
DXY is consolidating the strong bullish move that began in early September, coinciding with a sharp increase in market expectations for further Fed tightening.
Whether you call it a symmetrical triangle or a bull pennant, the price has now tested both sides of the structure on several occasions, with the trading range continuing to narrow as bullish momentum cools. The GBP/USD pair attracts some buyers for the third straight day, trading around mid-1.3200s during the Asians session on Monday, though it remains confined in a familiar range held over the past three weeks or so.
The recent minor pullback in US bond yields from multi-year highs keeps US Dollar bulls on the defensive, which, in turn, is seen as a key factor acting as a tailwind for the GBP/USD pair. Meanwhile, UK Chancellor John Healey repeated his commitment to strict fiscal discipline during his upcoming debut budget on October 28, turning out to be another factor supporting the British Pound (GBP) and the currency pair.
Traders, however, might opt to wait for Healey's speech at the annual meetings of the IMF and World Bank in Bangkok. Traders will further take cues from the Bank of England (BoE) Governor Andrew Bailey and the US Federal Reserve (Fed) Chair Kevin Warsh's speeches on Friday. Apart from this, the monthly UK GDP report and the latest US inflation figures should provide a fresh impetus to the GBP/USD pair.
In the meantime, persistent geopolitical uncertainties stemming from the US-Iran standoff could help limit losses for the safe-haven buck. In fact, tensions in the Middle East deepened on Sunday after Iran’s top security official declared Washington’s response to its proposal for reopening the strategic Strait of Hormuz insufficient, while US President Donald Trump considers renewed military strikes against Tehran.
This might hold back traders from placing aggressive bearish bets on the Greenback amid relatively thin liquidity on the back of a holiday in the US and keep a lid on any further appreciation for the GBP/USD pair. Hence, it will be prudent to wait for strong follow-through buying and a breakout through a short-term range before confirming that the currency pair has bottomed out and positioning for further gains.
The recent range-bound price action witnessed over the past three weeks or so could be categorized as a bearish consolidation phase against the backdrop of the decline from the August swing high. Moreover, the GBP/USD pair trades beneath the 100-period Simple Moving Average (SMA) dynamic barrier on the 4-hour chart, suggesting that rallies remain capped as sellers retain the advantage while spot prices stay below this barrier.
The said barrier is pegged near 1.3260 and is followed by the top boundary of the trading range, around 1.3300. Sustained strength above the latter is needed to ease bearish pressure and open the way toward higher levels. On the downside, bears might await some follow-through weakness below 1.3180 before placing fresh bets and positioning for an extension of the downfall from the August monthly swing high near 1.3675.
(The technical analysis of this story was written with the help of an AI tool. Know more.)
The Pound Sterling (GBP) is the oldest currency in the world (886 AD) and the official currency of the United Kingdom. It is the fourth most traded unit for foreign exchange (FX) in the world, accounting for 12% of all transactions, averaging $630 billion a day, according to 2022 data. Its key trading pairs are GBP/USD, also known as ‘Cable’, which accounts for 11% of FX, GBP/JPY, or the ‘Dragon’ as it is known by traders (3%), and EUR/GBP (2%). The Pound Sterling is issued by the Bank of England (BoE).
The single most important factor influencing the value of the Pound Sterling is monetary policy decided by the Bank of England. The BoE bases its decisions on whether it has achieved its primary goal of “price stability” – a steady inflation rate of around 2%. Its primary tool for achieving this is the adjustment of interest rates. When inflation is too high, the BoE will try to rein it in by raising interest rates, making it more expensive for people and businesses to access credit. This is generally positive for GBP, as higher interest rates make the UK a more attractive place for global investors to park their money. When inflation falls too low it is a sign economic growth is slowing. In this scenario, the BoE will consider lowering interest rates to cheapen credit so businesses will borrow more to invest in growth-generating projects.
Data releases gauge the health of the economy and can impact the value of the Pound Sterling. Indicators such as GDP, Manufacturing and Services PMIs, and employment can all influence the direction of the GBP. A strong economy is good for Sterling. Not only does it attract more foreign investment but it may encourage the BoE to put up interest rates, which will directly strengthen GBP. Otherwise, if economic data is weak, the Pound Sterling is likely to fall.
Another significant data release for the Pound Sterling is the Trade Balance. This indicator measures the difference between what a country earns from its exports and what it spends on imports over a given period. If a country produces highly sought-after exports, its currency will benefit purely from the extra demand created from foreign buyers seeking to purchase these goods. Therefore, a positive net Trade Balance strengthens a currency and vice versa for a negative balance.

West Texas Intermediate (WTI) declines after two days of gains, trading around $90.00 per barrel during Asian hours on Monday. However, crude oil prices may regain ground following deadly attacks on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport, which has prompted United States (US) President Donald Trump to consider joining Saudi Arabia in retaliating against Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen. The Riyadh airport was targeted again on Sunday by Houthi militants, just a day after a previous strike killed 12 people and injured more than 300.
Adding to regional supply risks, a drone struck an oil tanker near the Sohar anchorage off Oman over the weekend, just outside the Strait of Hormuz, highlighting ongoing vulnerabilities despite signs of higher crude exports from the Persian Gulf.
Meanwhile, geopolitical developments surrounding Russia and Ukraine remain uncertain. President Trump claimed that Russia and Ukraine have agreed to an "energy ceasefire," though he provided no specific details.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy noted that while he discussed an energy ceasefire with leaders from Canada, Finland, and NATO, he was unaware of any agreement between Ukraine and Russia announced by Trump. However, Zelenskyy added that if Moscow were to agree to such a ceasefire, Kyiv would accept it.
US Department of Energy announced the approval of an emergency exchange involving up to 4 million barrels of crude oil from strategic reserves. This measure is intended to help mitigate supply disruptions caused by Hurricane Isaias.
Systematic flows whipsawed as WTI hovers around key CTA trigger
According to TD Securities, systematic players are struggling to find direction as “CTAs [are] whipsawing in WTI,” with recent price action underscoring that “the $90/bbl region is proving to be an important CTA level in WTI crude.” The bank notes that this zone has become a pivotal reference point for trend-following strategies, as crude repeatedly oscillates around it and triggers rapid shifts in positioning.
WTI Oil FAQs
WTI Oil is a type of Crude Oil sold on international markets. The WTI stands for West Texas Intermediate, one of three major types including Brent and Dubai Crude. WTI is also referred to as “light” and “sweet” because of its relatively low gravity and sulfur content respectively. It is considered a high quality Oil that is easily refined. It is sourced in the United States and distributed via the Cushing hub, which is considered “The Pipeline Crossroads of the World”. It is a benchmark for the Oil market and WTI price is frequently quoted in the media.
Like all assets, supply and demand are the key drivers of WTI Oil price. As such, global growth can be a driver of increased demand and vice versa for weak global growth. Political instability, wars, and sanctions can disrupt supply and impact prices. The decisions of OPEC, a group of major Oil-producing countries, is another key driver of price. The value of the US Dollar influences the price of WTI Crude Oil, since Oil is predominantly traded in US Dollars, thus a weaker US Dollar can make Oil more affordable and vice versa.
The weekly Oil inventory reports published by the American Petroleum Institute (API) and the Energy Information Agency (EIA) impact the price of WTI Oil. Changes in inventories reflect fluctuating supply and demand. If the data shows a drop in inventories it can indicate increased demand, pushing up Oil price. Higher inventories can reflect increased supply, pushing down prices. API’s report is published every Tuesday and EIA’s the day after. Their results are usually similar, falling within 1% of each other 75% of the time. The EIA data is considered more reliable, since it is a government agency.
OPEC (Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries) is a group of 12 Oil-producing nations who collectively decide production quotas for member countries at twice-yearly meetings. Their decisions often impact WTI Oil prices. When OPEC decides to lower quotas, it can tighten supply, pushing up Oil prices. When OPEC increases production, it has the opposite effect. OPEC+ refers to an expanded group that includes ten extra non-OPEC members, the most notable of which is Russia.

articles.full_text:
HM Treasury is currently making annual payments to cover the Asset Purchase Facility’s losses as the Bank of England’s programme of quantitative easing is unwound. This chapter summarises how the APF works and how flows between the APF and HM Treasury impact the public finances.
Key findings
- Since 2009, the Bank of England has bought significant quantities of government bonds, and some corporate bonds, through its quantitative easing (QE) programme. These are held in the Asset Purchase Facility (APF), a legally separate entity which is indemnified by HM Treasury. Between 2009 and 2022, the APF was making profits and a policy choice was made to send these immediately to HM Treasury. These had amounted to £124 billion in total by Q3 2022.
- Since then, the APF has been reducing its holdings (quantitative tightening, QT) and has begun making losses. We estimate that payments from HM Treasury to cover APF losses in 2026–27 will be £19 billion. This is roughly equivalent to total spending on police services in England and Wales. By early next year, the government is expected to have roughly broken even on the QE/QT programme in a narrow accounting sense, but with further losses to come.
- Economic changes since March have increased the APF’s projected losses over the next five years. A higher expectation for Bank Rate increases the cost of financing the loans that initially funded the APF’s bond purchases, and higher yields on government debt decrease the value of the government bonds that the APF decides to sell. The Bank of England also announced changes to the QT programme last month: slowing the pace of bond sales, and concentrating sales on bonds that are set to mature between 2035 and 2049. Together, we estimate that changes since March mean that total APF losses will be around £5 billion higher in each of 2026–27 and 2027–28. Largely as a result of the changes announced by the Bank, total losses are expected to fall to £13 billion in 2030–31 – £6 billion less than we expected in March.
- Only a portion of these losses affect the fiscal aggregates that are targeted by the government’s fiscal rules. We estimate the changes since March are likely to reduce the current budget surplus – revenues net of day-to-day spending – by £3.4 billion. In contrast, we expect them to leave the government’s preferred measure of debt (PSNFL) roughly unchanged in the same year. Importantly, under current arrangements, the whole of any losses results in a cash transfer from HM Treasury to the APF. This can be funded through higher government borrowing, higher taxes or reduced government spending on other things.
- Other ways of managing these losses are possible, and have international precedents. Changing arrangements between HM Treasury and the Bank would not be a free lunch: all options would amount to reallocating losses either through time or between different groups in the economy. However, given the extent of the costs in the near term, now is the time for an open and informed discussion of these arrangements.
4.1 Introduction
In response to the financial crisis of 2008 and subsequent shocks, the Bank of England, along with other global central banks, bought significant quantities of government bonds, in a policy known as quantitative easing (QE). More recently, it has been reversing this through quantitative tightening (QT), allowing its holdings of these bonds to mature without replacing them and actively selling some back to investors on financial markets.
Over the course of this policy, the Bank has made gains and losses, which have resulted in payments to and from HM Treasury. The technical arrangements surrounding this are complex, but they are important, because the exact arrangement affects the government’s fiscal position.
In this chapter, we explain how the QE/QT programme is operating and describe the recent changes announced by the Bank. We discuss how gains and losses currently feed through into transfers to and from HM Treasury and impact the public finances, and how the scale of these transfers is set to change in the coming years. Finally, we discuss whether there are changes the government could make to its arrangements with the Bank which would impact the fiscal arithmetic in the coming months and years.
Box 4.1. How do bonds work?
One way that companies or governments can borrow is by issuing bonds. Effectively this involves selling IOUs for future payments. When issuing a bond, the issuer sets a term (e.g. five years) and can then include commitments to two different types of future payment:a
- a coupon: an amount paid at regular intervals (e.g. every six months) over the life of the bond;
- a redemption value: an amount paid at the end of the bond’s term (at maturity).
For example, a government or company could issue a bond that lasts ten years and promises to provide £5 each year for those years, and a further £100 when it reaches maturity.
When government issues (sells) a bond to a lender, it receives an up-front payment – the price. The price of bonds reflects the balance of demand and supply for that specific type of bond. If lots of investors want to buy a particular type of bond, it might have a high price; if there are low levels of demand relative to supply, it might sell for a low price. The demand and supply for a given bond will depend both on economic conditions, such as central bank policy rates and inflation, and on the specific characteristics of the bond issuer.
The higher the price of a given bond, the lower the effective interest rate – the yield – on that bond. Take a simple example of a bond that only lasts one year, offers no coupons and has a redemption value of £100 after that year. If it is sold for £90, the lender gives up £90 immediately for a promise of £100 a year later. They receive interest of £10, so the effective interest rate is 11% (£10 divided by £90). If instead the same bond sold for £95, the lender would only receive £5 of interest after a year, so the effective interest rate would be 5.3% (£5/£95).
As well as a primary market for bonds – in which lenders buy bonds directly from bond issuers (in this case, government) – there is also a secondary market for bonds. A lender who has already bought a bond can sell it on. In doing so, the original lender receives cash immediately in return for giving up any remaining coupon payments on the bond and the future redemption value.
a In most cases, the coupon and redemption value of a bond are fixed cash amounts. There are also inflation-linked bonds where the value of the coupon payment and the redemption value are automatically uprated with inflation.
4.2 A brief history of quantitative easing and quantitative tightening
Quantitative easing (QE) was rolled out in 2009 during the financial crisis to help stimulate the economy out of recession and bring inflation up to the Bank of England’s 2% target. It was an untested tool and there was limited precedent to inform its design. In order to let the Bank of England focus on its aim of stabilising the economy, rather than concerns of the potential profit and loss inherent in holding a large portfolio, the Bank and the government agreed that the bonds purchased would be held in a legally separate entity rather than directly on the balance sheet of the Bank of England. This entity was termed the Asset Purchase Facility (APF). The government then guaranteed, or indemnified, the financial position of this facility, meaning HM Treasury would make good on any losses that were incurred.
The APF then purchased predominantly government bonds, as well as some corporate bonds, from the market. It funded these purchases with a loan from the Bank of England, on which it is required to pay the Bank of England’s base rate – like a tracker mortgage. The Bank of England in turn financed these loans by creating new money, in the form of reserves held by commercial banks, on which it pays interest at the Bank of England’s base rate.
When QE was initiated, the UK was in recession and inflation was below the Bank’s target, so the Bank wanted to stimulate additional demand in the economy. By buying government and corporate bonds, the APF aimed to reduce interest rates across the economy, reducing the cost of borrowing for both households and firms, with the aim of stimulating additional investment and consumption.
QE was used to support the economy after the 2008 global financial crisis, following the 2016 Brexit shock and in response to the 2020 pandemic-induced slowdown. The APF’s bond holdings peaked in 2021 when it owned £875 billion in gilts (around a third of total government debt) and a further £20 billion in UK corporate bonds (Ramsden, 2023).
QE was always intended to be a temporary intervention. Since 2022, the Bank of England has been ‘unwinding’ it, reducing the stock of bonds it holds in the APF. This has become known as quantitative tightening (QT).
The Bank has carried out QT in two ways. First, it has let some bonds reach maturity. When this happens, the APF receives the redemption value from the bond issuer and pays back the initial loan it took out from the Bank of England. This is termed passive unwind. Second, the Bank has sold some bonds on the market. A Canadian cybersecurity executive who specializes in negotiating with ransomware hackers has reportedly been arrested on federal charges in Pennsylvania.
Edward Dubrovsky, 54, was arrested Thursday in the Philadelphia area, according to federal court documents cited by Reuters. The arrest comes as the FBI investigates ShinyHunters, a hacking group that recently claimed to have stolen information concerning nearly every FBI employee. Authorities have not publicly confirmed whether Dubrovsky's arrest is connected to that investigation.
FBI Director Kash Patel announced Friday in a post on X that agents had arrested another suspected co-conspirator of ShinyHunters, the group believed to be responsible for a recent incident involving the FBI's jobs website.
"Our agents in the field have arrested another suspected co-conspirator of the ShinyHunters group – the group believed to be responsible for the recent FBIjobs.gov incident, which occurred on a platform managed by a third-party vendor," Patel wrote.
Patel said the arrest was the latest involving the network in a matter of days as the FBI works to dismantle the group and pursue additional leads. He did not identify the arrested suspect by name, and authorities have not publicly confirmed whether Dubrovsky is the individual referenced in his statement.
Federal court records filed in the Eastern District of Pennsylvania list charges involving conspiracy to threaten the confidentiality of information to extort money and interference with commerce, Reuters reported.
The specific conduct underlying the federal allegations remains unclear because the criminal case in the Eastern District of Texas is sealed.
A federal court order issued Thursday in Pennsylvania shows that prosecutors requested the defendant's detention and that a judge ordered him held pending a detention hearing in the Eastern District of Texas.
A separate order issued Friday directed the U.S. Marshals Service to transport the defendant to Texas for further proceedings.
According to the Federal Bureau of Prisons' online inmate locator, Dubrovsky is listed as being held at the Federal Detention Center in Philadelphia. His release date is listed as unknown.
Dubrovsky's professional background includes negotiating with cybercriminals over ransom demands, according to his LinkedIn profile.
His profile identifies him as being affiliated with CyberSteward, a cybersecurity firm that advertises services involving negotiations with threat actors, cyber extortion and settlement facilitation.

articles.title: American Farm Bureau Federation on U.S.-China Trade Framework: What We Know Now, Say Lower Tariffs Can Help U.S. Products Compete, But They Don't Guarantee Sales - Sierra Sun Times
articles.summary: American Farm Bureau Federation on U.S.-China Trade Framework: What We Know Now, Say Lower Tariffs Can Help U.S. Products Compete, But They Don't Guarantee Sales  Sierra Sun Times
articles.full_text:
Key Takeaways
- China’s list of goods covered under the new “30-for-30" trade framework includes major U.S. agricultural products such as beef, pork, poultry, dairy, corn, wheat, rice, sorghum and specialty crops, but whole soybeans are excluded.
- The roughly $30 billion figure reflects the value of products covered by the framework. Lower tariffs can help U.S. products compete, but they don't guarantee sales.
- The benefits for farmers and ranchers will depend on how far tariffs are reduced, how quickly changes take effect and whether the new agricultural working group can resolve non-tariff market-access barriers.
October 11, 2026 - By Faith Parum, Ph.D - The United States and China have taken another step toward easing trade barriers, each identifying roughly $30 billion in goods for tariff reductions. This list comes from the newly established U.S.-China Board of Trade. For U.S. agriculture, the agreement covers a wide range of products, from beef and pork to corn, wheat, dairy and specialty crops. However, this is not a purchase commitment. Several important details, including final tariff rates, the timing of implementation and the exclusion of whole soybeans, limit how much can be concluded about its near-term impact on U.S. farm exports.
On Sept. 27, the White House released the first product lists under the new “30-for-30” framework. The two governments set lists based on 2024 bilateral trade: 1,619 U.S. products for potential tariff reductions entering China and 77 Chinese products entering the United States. The actual rate of tariff reductions is yet to determined. Both countries will need to announce reduction rates and specify how they will be implemented.
Agriculture is Prominent on China’s List
Agricultural products make up a significant portion of China’s list. Covered products include beef, pork, lamb, poultry and offal; dairy products such as cheese, butter and cream; wheat, barley, corn, rice and sorghum; fruits, vegetables, beans and mushrooms; edible oils, juices and processed foods; as well as seafood, pet food, tobacco and forest products.
China's Ministry of Commerce has said about 90% of covered products are expected to see tariffs cut to most-favored-nation (MFN) rates, the standard tariffs China charges World Trade Organization (WTO) members without a free trade agreement. That would remove the retaliatory duties added during the trade dispute but not eliminate tariffs, so competitors with free trade agreements, like Australia and New Zealand, could still pay less. Notably for U.S. agriculture, though, it would return covered products to tariff rates equal to competitors in South America like Brazil and Argentina. Specific reductions and implementation dates have not been released.
However, one notable agriculture product is left out. Whole soybeans. Soybeans have historically been one of the top agricultural exports to China, but they are not included in this round of proposed tariff reductions. Soybean oil and some other soybean-derived products are covered; however, China is primarily a whole soybean importer, owing to a mature domestic crush industry. In late 2025 and spring 2026, the administration announced separate purchase commitments with China, including at least 25 million metric tons of soybeans and at least $17 billion in agricultural purchases annually in 2026, 2027 and 2028. This latest agreement does not include any purchase commitments.
Trade Has Fallen Sharply
Historically, China has been a top trading partner for U.S. agriculture. However, that has fallen amid the ongoing negotiations and trade tensions. USDA reports that U.S. agricultural exports to China fell 66% in 2025 to $8.4 billion, dropping China to the sixth-largest U.S. agricultural export market. USDA attributed much of that decline to reciprocal tariffs and weaker Chinese demand for U.S. soybeans. USDA’s May trade forecast projected fiscal year 2026 agricultural exports to China at about $12 billion, compared with $16.2 billion in fiscal year 2025.
The new agreement to lower tariffs on products included in the 30-for-30 framework may improve the competitiveness of U.S. commodities. For products such as meat, dairy, grains and specialty crops, even modest tariff reductions can narrow the price gap between U.S. products and competing supplies from countries with more favorable trade arrangements.
However, there are other factors that impact trade outside of tariffs. Chinese purchases will still depend on domestic consumption, commodity prices, exchange rates, production conditions and competition from other exporters. Brazil, Australia, New Zealand and other major agricultural suppliers will continue competing for market share. In many commodities, U.S. producers also face non-tariff barriers that cannot be resolved simply by reducing an import duty.
The Agricultural Working Group
The announcement also included the creation of a working group within the China Board of Trade that will specifically focus on agricultural market access barriers. The White House described the group as a mechanism for addressing impediments to agricultural trade beyond tariffs.
Agricultural exporters routinely face sanitary and phytosanitary requirements, facility registrations, onerous biotechnology approval processes, product eligibility rules and other regulatory requirements that can limit market access even when tariff rates are competitive. Continued negotiations through a standing agricultural working group could provide a venue for addressing those barriers product by product.
What it Means for Agriculture
The 30-for-30 framework represents potential improvement in market access for U.S. agriculture, particularly livestock products, grains, dairy and specialty crops. However, the agreement does not guarantee additional purchases. The $30 billion figure reflects the 2024 trade value of goods included in the broader framework, not a Chinese commitment to purchase $30 billion of U.S. products.
For farmers and ranchers, the real test is how far tariffs fall, how quickly the cuts take effect, whether regulatory barriers are addressed and, ultimately, whether ships leave U.S. ports loaded with American farm products bound for China.
Source: American Farm Bureau Federation

Net selling pressure from foreign investors and a sideways trading scenario are leaning towards a decline.
Stock market week 12-16/10: Awaiting differentiated capital flows from Q3 earnings season.
After a week of sideways trading around the August lows, the Vietnamese stock market enters the new week with a cautious sentiment. Analysts believe the VN-Index will continue its search for equilibrium, while the Q3 earnings season is expected to be the main catalyst driving capital flows to differentiate specific sectors.
The trading week from October 5th to 9th concluded with a clear tug-of-war, as the VN-Index recovered in the first two sessions but quickly weakened and declined in the following three consecutive sessions. The index continued to fluctuate around its August lows, accompanied by deep divergence among industry groups. Large-cap stocks failed to maintain sustained upward momentum, especially as the Vingroup group stalled and bank stocks faced profit-taking pressure.
Assessing market developments, Mr. Nguyen Tan Phong, a securities analyst at Pinetree, believes that the VN-Index has yet to escape its short-term correction trend. Capital is showing signs of withdrawing from large-cap stocks to seek opportunities in small and medium-sized stocks with unique business stories. For example, on October 8th, just two stocks, VHM and VIC, pulled the index down by more than 7 points. In addition, net selling pressure from foreign investors continues to be a major obstacle, with the selling streak extending to 13 consecutive sessions. Negative international macroeconomic factors also contributed, with Brent crude oil prices exceeding $104 per barrel and 10-year US Treasury yields remaining at their highest level since 2002, creating pressure for capital withdrawal from emerging markets.
Forecasting for the trading week of October 12-16, Pinetree experts predict that the VN-Index will likely maintain a sideways downtrend within a narrow range of 1,700 to 1,760 points. The net selling by foreign investors is unlikely to end anytime soon, as the Fed meeting minutes indicate the agency is still open to further interest rate hikes. A rare bright spot comes from the solid domestic macroeconomic foundation, with Q3 GDP growth reaching 9.95%. However, Mr. Phong warns that the biggest risk currently is the high domestic interest rate environment coupled with inflationary pressure due to rising energy costs. Regarding investment strategy, he recommends that investors proactively reduce their stock holdings to a defensive level, only taking advantage of short rallies to optimize profits rather than expecting a sustained upward trend.
Expectations of bargain hunting demand and opportunities from four core industry groups.
From a more optimistic perspective, expert Nguyen Anh Khoa assessed that the decline of the VN-Index has shown signs of weakening, although it remains within the corrective trend formed since mid-September. Looking at the long-term timeframe, the market has mainly been moving sideways within a wide range since the beginning of the year. With the total market trading volume increasing by about 8% if block trades are excluded, Mr. Khoa believes that there has been a localized improvement in capital flow in some stocks that have fallen sharply, such as PNJ or NVL, although this is not enough to confirm a broad reversal signal.
Regarding the issue of net selling by foreign investors, with cumulative value exceeding VND 100 trillion since the beginning of 2026, Mr. Khoa acknowledged that this will continue to exert psychological pressure in the context of an unfavorable global macroeconomic environment. However, this pressure is expected to gradually decrease after FTSE Russell officially upgrades Vietnam to the secondary emerging market group from September 21, 2026. The roadmap to include Vietnamese stocks in global indices, extending to 2027, will open up opportunities to attract capital from international investment funds, helping to gradually balance the trading volume.
Ahead of the Q3 earnings season, Mr. Khoa recommends that investors maintain a moderate proportion of stocks in their portfolios and avoid rushing to invest. Instead, capital should focus on four sectors with promising profit prospects: retail, banking, construction materials, and oil and gas. The expert emphasized that good business results are only a necessary condition; investors need to choose stocks with reasonable valuations, long-term growth prospects, and invest gradually rather than chasing prices to manage risk in a market where a clear trend has not yet been established.

U.S. equity markets posted broad weekly gains for the period from October 5 to October 11, 2026, with benchmark indexes achieving new record highs before experiencing mid-week volatility. The S&P 500 rose 1.2% over the reporting period, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 0.9%. The Nasdaq Composite lagged with a 0.6% advance as semiconductor and mega-cap technology shares faced profit-taking. In style rotation, value and broad-market equities led the advance, with the equal-weighted S&P 500 outperforming the market-cap benchmark by rising 1.6%. Smaller capitalization equities underperformed, as the Russell 2000 index fell between 0.5% and 1.0% under the weight of higher borrowing costs. Sector performance showed nine of eleven S&P sectors advancing, led by defensive and energy segments including Utilities, Consumer Staples, and Energy, while Technology was among the few declining sectors.
Monetary policy dynamics and corporate announcements served as primary market drivers. The release of Federal Reserve meeting minutes showed a unanimous vote for the September rate hike to 3.75 percent to 4 percent, though softer nonfarm payroll data reduced market expectations for an October rate hike to below 20%. Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller noted during an October 8 address in Istanbul that upside risks to inflation remain a key concern, with core personal consumption expenditures inflation remaining sticky between 2.5% and 3.0%. In corporate news, third-quarter earnings season kicked off alongside strategic commercial deals, including Constellation Energy contracting power delivery to Google, which provided support to energy and industrial shares.
Market sentiment demonstrated moderate stabilization despite pressure from the bond market, with the CBOE Volatility Index edging down to 15.41. Equity fund flows and positioning indicators pointed to cautious repositioning, as the Fear & Greed Index rose from 31 to 45 into neutral territory, even though broader market breadth metrics remained cautious. Institutional flows favored high-dividend defensive sectors and equal-weighted indexes, reflecting a strategy to insulate portfolios against elevated risk-free yields. Investors trimmed momentum positions in high-multiple technology and semiconductor stocks, redirecting liquidity toward value segments that offer attractive intrinsic valuations and resilient balance sheets.
The overall market behavior reflects a late-cycle phase characterized by a widening divergence between corporate earnings resilience and restrictive macro-financial conditions. Resilient corporate profitability and secular artificial intelligence spending continue to support large-cap equity valuations, allowing benchmark indexes to trade near historic highs despite 10-year Treasury yields reaching levels not seen in over two decades. However, the persistent drag of elevated interest rates on small-cap stocks, stagnant housing activity, and weakening consumer sentiment suggests that the broad economy faces ongoing headwinds. The equity market is navigating an environment where strong micro fundamentals are balancing out macro policy tightening.

Looking ahead to the coming week, financial markets will focus on pivotal macroeconomic releases and the formal acceleration of the third-quarter earnings calendar. Key economic releases include the September Consumer Price Index and Producer Price Index reports, which will provide crucial evidence on whether inflationary pressures are continuing to broaden. Investors will also monitor monthly retail sales data and regional manufacturing surveys to gauge consumer spending health. On the corporate front, major Wall Street financial institutions will kick off third-quarter bank earnings, setting the tone for corporate profitability, net interest margin trends, and credit loss provision expectations.
Market price action in the upcoming week will likely be dictated by the interaction between inflation data and Treasury yield movements. If incoming inflation data prints higher than anticipated, bond yields could re-test multi-year highs, creating valuation pressure on high-duration growth equities and reigniting policy tightening concerns for the December FOMC meeting. Conversely, if inflation shows signs of moderation and initial bank earnings exceed expectations, equities could extend their broad-based rotation, allowing value and cyclical sectors to maintain momentum while helping major benchmarks digest high risk-free interest rates.
From a strategy perspective, institutional investors are advised to maintain a balanced and quality-oriented allocation framework. Equity portfolios should feature an overweight tilt toward high-quality value and defensive sectors, including Healthcare, Consumer Staples, and Utilities, which offer attractive dividend yields and earnings stability in a high-rate environment. Exposure to mega-cap technology leadership should be retained selectively to participate in artificial intelligence growth trends, but concentration risk should be managed by utilizing equal-weighted index strategies. Maintaining moderate cash reserves will also allow investors to capitalize on potential volatility spikes surrounding economic data releases.
Key market risk factors requiring close attention include potential upside spikes in inflation driven by volatile energy markets and ongoing Middle East geopolitical conflicts. A sustained break of the 10-year Treasury yield above recent highs would increase corporate borrowing costs and pressure equity market valuation multiples. Additional downside risks include potential credit quality deterioration reported in bank earnings, downward revisions to fourth-quarter corporate earnings guidance, and further declines in household consumer sentiment that could signal a sharper retrenchment in broad consumer spending.

articles.full_text:
The meetings from October 12 to 18 will bring together financial leaders in Bangkok. Food security and funding for African economies are on the agenda.
The annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank will open on Monday, October 12, in Bangkok, focusing on food security and funding for African economies. The meetings will run until October 18, as the World Bank anticipates a resurgence of inflation in sub-Saharan Africa despite stronger growth.
On the eve of these meetings, World Bank President Ajay Banga told Reuters in an interview published on October 11 that the institution is discussing potential crisis assistance with 30 to 40 countries. These discussions are focused on energy shocks and rising prices caused by the war in the Middle East.
In June, the World Bank had presented a framework that could mobilize $50 to $60 billion through its existing instruments, including $25 billion in pre-arranged financing. This support can fund targeted assistance for vulnerable households and provide liquidity to businesses and farms.
The IMF schedule includes the presentation of its new global economic outlook on Tuesday, October 13, followed by a press briefing from its Africa department on Thursday, October 15. The meetings will also address debt, financial stability, and ways to mobilize private capital.
In its regional report published on October 6, the World Bank projects sub-Saharan growth of 4.3% in 2026, up from 4.1% in 2025. However, it also anticipates a rise in median inflation from 3.7% to 5.5%, driven by increased costs of fuels, fertilizers, and food products.
The burden of debt repayment continues to limit available resources for health, education, and infrastructure, according to the institution. A decline in development aid exacerbates this constraint. Furthermore, economic activity remains insufficient to create enough jobs and significantly reduce extreme poverty.
Burkina Faso’s Finance Minister, Aboubakar Nacanabo, is scheduled to participate in a discussion on food security on October 15, alongside his counterparts from Djibouti and Somalia. The debate will focus on protecting vulnerable households from rising food and transport costs, as well as targeting aid in fragile, import-dependent countries.
Several African countries are entering these meetings following new financing negotiations. The IMF announced on October 8 a technical agreement of $203 million with Niger, spanning 38 months, and on October 9, a proposed program of $1.472 billion over three years with Zambia. Both agreements are subject to approval by the Fund’s board of directors; the Zambian program also requires the implementation of prior measures.

articles.title: Trump establishes committee to investigate Federal Reserve’s Lisa Cook in latest effort to fire her - Jamaica Gleaner
articles.summary: Trump establishes committee to investigate Federal Reserve’s Lisa Cook in latest effort to fire her  Jamaica Gleaner
articles.full_text:
Trump establishes committee to investigate Federal Reserve’s Lisa Cook in latest effort to fire her
Loading article...
US President Donald Trump opened another chapter in his effort to fire Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook Friday by establishing a “committee of inquiry” to investigate allegations that she made false statements in mortgage applications.
The inquiry will include a hearing at the White House November 5, Trump said in a written memo, that Cook ‘shall’ attend to answer questions from the committee. The hearing wouldn’t be public but a transcript would be published, the memo said.
Trump’s extraordinary demand that Cook testify before the committee will likely renew concerns about threats to the Federal Reserve’s independence. The president has repeatedly called for the central bank to cut its key interest rate, but just last month, the Fed raised it instead, led by Chairman Kevin Warsh, whom Trump appointed earlier this year.
Trump’s attempts to fire Cook from the Fed’s seven-member board of governors represent the first time in the central bank’s 113-year history that a president has sought to remove a Fed governor. Cook was appointed by former President Joe Biden and is the first Black woman on the Fed’s board. Trump’s attacks on her followed other efforts to oust or indict Black officials, such as New York Attorney General Letitia James and General Charles Q. Brown, the former chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff.
“As President, it is my job to ensure the laws are faithfully executed, including by firing subordinates who cannot be trusted to tell the truth and follow the law,” Trump wrote in the memorandum.
Cook’s attorneys, Abbe Lowell and Norman Eisen, said they were considering having Cook appear at the November 5 hearing and respond to the charges.
“We have engaged with the White House to evaluate whether the process proposed has a possibility of being a genuine one and not simply a box checking exercise,” Lowell and Eisen said in a statement. “Governor Cook welcomes the opportunity to present the facts so she can clear her name and demonstrate there is no legal basis to fire her.”
The “committee of inquiry” will be composed of Kevin Hassett, the president’s top economic adviser, who has frequently echoed Trump’s criticisms of the Fed; Keith Sonderling, the acting director of the Office of Government Ethics, whom the president has also appointed to lead the Labor Department, and Andrea Lucas, the chair of the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, whom Trump appointed in November 2025.
Fraud accusation
Trump initially tried to fire Cook in August 2025 after alleging she had committed mortgage fraud by declaring two different properties to be her “primary” residence in mortgage applications in 2021. Mortgages on primary homes can often receive a lower interest rate or other beneficial terms.
Cook has denied any wrongdoing and has not been charged with a crime. Lowell and Eisen have previously said Cook committed an “inadvertent error” and did refer to one of the properties as a vacation home in other documents.
“An inadvertent error is not fraud, as the President and a third of his cabinet should know because they reportedly did the same thing,” Lowell and Eisen said in August.
The Federal Reserve declined to comment on Trump’s announcement.
Trump and some of his economic advisers have blamed the Fed’s broader rate-setting committee, which includes 12 voting members and 19 officials in total, for forcing last month’s rate hike, even though it followed comments by Warsh in August that signaled higher rates were likely. As a member of the board of governors, Cook is also one of the 12 voting members of the committee. The vote to lift rates September 16 was unanimous.
The move also follows a Supreme Court ruling in June that Cook could keep her job after Trump sought to fire her last year. That ruling included a footnote that said nothing prevented Trump from “trying again” as long as she was given proper notice and an opportunity to respond to the charges.
Trump said the committee of inquiry will seek to establish whether there is “cause” to fire Cook, as required under the law governing the Fed. The Supreme Court said in June that a for-cause firing required an alleged offense that was serious and related to an official’s job.
Scott Alvarez, formerly the chief counsel for the Fed, said that President William Howard Taft set up a similar commission in 1912 to remove two officials from an independent agency. The commission created by Trump goes beyond the type of process the Supreme Court said was needed to fire Cook.
-AP
“It’s an attempt to show that he’s really giving Cook as much process as possible,” Alvarez said.
Still, the allegations against Cook don’t appear to meet the “for cause” standard set out by the Supreme Court, Alvarez said.
Other analysts said that Trump will likely use the process to ultimately fire Cook.
“We do not see why the White House would start this process if it were not trying to create a way to justify removing Cook from her job,” Jaret Seiberg, managing director of TD Cowen’s Washington Research Group, said in a note to clients.

Wall Street, and the crypto market that often moves with it, is heading into a packed stretch.
Five US events, from hiring numbers to two inflation reports and a talk by Fed Chair Kevin Warsh, could shape what the central bank does with interest rates next.
Here is the Fed interest news today, explained in plain words, with every number taken from official sources.
Source: Post by Bull theory

The days ahead open with the ADP weekly report, which shows how many jobs private companies are adding.
In its latest release on October 6, ADP Research reported that private employers added an average of 23,750 jobs weekly across the four weeks ending September 19.
ADP also said hiring sped up for the fifth straight reading. The next update is due Tuesday, October 13.
ADP produces the report with the Stanford Digital Economy Lab and publishes it on Tuesday mornings at 8:15 a.m. Eastern Time.
The recent trend is clear:
Ending August 22: 12,250 jobs weekly
Ending September 5: 20,000 jobs weekly
Ending September 12: 22,500 jobs weekly
Ending September 19: 23,750 jobs weekly
That means the latest figure is 18.75% higher than the reading from two weeks earlier.
ADP notes these numbers are early estimates and can change as more data comes in.
Stronger hiring can make the Fed more careful about moving on rates, while a sudden slowdown can change the mood quickly.
Wednesday brings the Consumer Price Index, the main measure of what everyday shoppers pay.
According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, prices climbed 0.4% last month and 3.4% over the last 12 months.
The BLS said gasoline was a key reason for the monthly jump.
The bureau also tracks a calmer version of inflation that leaves out food and energy, because those two can swing sharply from month to month. That version gained 0.3% and 2.4% over the year.
The September report arrives on October 14 at 8:30 a.m. Eastern Time. It will show whether price pressure is easing or building again, which is why many people searching for fed interest news today are watching this release most closely.
On Thursday, the Producer Price Index shows how much prices are changing for the businesses that make and sell goods and services.
The BLS reported that this measure rose 0.4% for the month and stands 5.4% higher over the past 12 months.
The details show where the pressure came from:
Goods: +1.1%
Services: +0.1%
Energy: +4.2%
Diesel fuel: +24.1%
Crude petroleum: +5.2%
These are early figures, and the BLS may revise them. Higher costs for businesses can slowly reach shoppers through higher prices, so another strong reading could add to worries about inflation.
The September report is scheduled for October 15 at 8:30 a.m. Eastern Time.
Also on Thursday, the Labor Department releases its weekly count of people filing for unemployment benefits for the first time.
This is often the quickest sign of whether companies are cutting staff. The latest Labor Department report showed 197,000 first-time claims for the period ending October 3, down 2,000 from the revised prior level.
A year earlier, the same period had 233,000 claims.The report also showed about 1.716 million people receiving benefits in the period ending September 26, an increase of 17,000.
The BLS jobs report put the unemployment rate at 4.2% in September. Low claims suggest layoffs remain limited for now, but one weak reading can change how the job market looks.
The week ends with Fed Chair Kevin Warsh, and investors will listen for any hint about the next interest rate decision.
Because his words can move markets within minutes, traders will compare his tone with the inflation and job numbers.
A firmer message on prices could raise worries about higher rates, while a calmer one could lift hopes for patience.
You can check the exact time and format of the appearance on the Federal Reserve speeches page.
For crypto readers following Fed interest news today, this matters because Bitcoin and other digital assets often react when rate expectations change.
This week packs hiring, inflation, layoffs, and a Fed Chair appearance into five days, so market swings are possible.
Strong jobs and hot prices could keep rate worries alive, while softer numbers could bring relief.
Official figures can be revised, so check each source link on release day for the final numbers. Stay tuned for the latest Fed interest news today as each report lands.

The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has kept the repo rate unchanged at 5.25%, with the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) unanimously voting to maintain the status quo and retain its neutral policy stance.
Announcing the decision, RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra acknowledged growing global uncertainties, including elevated crude oil prices, supply chain disruptions, geopolitical tensions, and the risk of a weak monsoon due to El-Nino.
While retail inflation remains below the RBI's 4% target, the central bank warned that price pressures could intensify in the coming quarters.
The RBI has cut the repo rate by a cumulative 100 basis points since February 2025, the most aggressive easing in years. The central bank has also projected FY27 GDP growth at 6.9% and raising its retail inflation forecast to 4.6%. Since then, wholesale inflation has surged to a three-and-a-half-year high, global oil prices have remained volatile due to US- Iran tensions, and the rupee has experienced sharp fluctuations against the US dollar.
Crude oil has since pulled back, down 21.8% in May to around $91 in hopes of a US-Iran memorandum of understanding that could reopen the Strait of Hormuz. That easing in oil prices appears to have removed pressure for any emergency rate action.

WASHINGTON -- The Federal Reserve's internal watchdog said Wednesday that the central bank has broadly mismanaged an expansive building renovation project but did not find any criminal violations, as alleged by Trump administration prosecutors.
A variety of missteps by the Fed's Board of Governors and staff inflated the cost of the $2.4 billion renovation, the Fed's inspector general said. The board did not secure a comprehensive cost estimate at the beginning of the project, nor did it nail down a maximum overall cost, a step that could have forced the building contractor to absorb the impact of inflation, the IG said in a 120-page report. Prices spiked after construction began in 2022.
"Our review found that the Board has not effectively managed and executed its ... contract and repeatedly deviated from its cost-management provisions," the report said.
The building project became a high-profile flashpoint in the Trump administration's efforts to pressure the Fed into cutting its key interest rate. President Donald Trump even visited the construction site last July, when then-Chairman Jerome Powell corrected Trump's estimate of the project's expected costs as the two stood in hard hats before TV cameras.
Criticism of the project also mounted in Congress, leading Powell to request in July 2025 that the inspector general, Michael Horowitz, investigate the renovation.
The building project then became the focus of a criminal investigation by Trump's Justice Department, specifically into whether Powell had committed perjury during brief testimony about the renovation before a Senate committee. That investigation was dropped in April after a judge quashed subpoenas issued by Jeanine Pirro, the U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia. Pirro said then she would await the outcome of the inspector general's investigation before deciding whether to take any further action.
"At no point during our evaluation did we find reasonable grounds to believe that a violation of federal criminal law had occurred requiring a referral to the U.S. Attorney General," the IG's report said.
Tim Lauer, a spokesperson for Pirro's office, said the report is under review.
Powell's term as chair ended in May, but he took the highly unusual step of remaining on the board as one of seven governors. His term as a governor lasts until January 2028. Powell said earlier this year he would remain on the board at least until he is convinced that Pirro's investigation is done. By keeping his seat, Powell has also prevented the Trump administration from filling another spot on the board.
Trump on Wednesday afternoon seized on the report to renew his call for Powell to resign from the Fed.
"He can't manage a Building, and he certainly shouldn't be allowed to manage his High Interest Rate Policy," Trump wrote on his social media site, Truth Social. "And no, I do not want this Building named after President Donald J. Trump, ME!"
Massachusetts Sen. Elizabeth Warren, the top Democrat on the Senate Banking Committee and a frequent critic of Powell's, said the report "confirmed that Trump lapdogs U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro and Attorney General Todd Blanche have no basis to restart the President's witch hunt against former Fed Chair Jerome Powell."
Current Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh, who took office last May, welcomed the IG's findings in a letter and said the General Services Administration, a federal agency that oversees most government buildings, would take on a consulting role with the Fed to help oversee the project.
He also said the Fed would engage an independent auditor to evaluate the building project and all its costs. The Fed, with the GSA, will review all the project's contracts and "pursue appropriate remedies," including seeking reimbursement for any work paid for but not performed, the letter said.
The report said that the construction costs to renovate two Fed buildings more than doubled from an original estimate of $921 million in February 2020 to $2.018 billion by December 2024. Construction is expected to last until December 2027, long past its originally slated completion date of mid-2024.
Some aspects of the project that were criticized by the Trump administration and Republican members of Congress for being luxurious -- water fountains, private elevators and marble facades -- were not significant drivers of the excessive costs of the project, the report said.
Instead, the IG said that a design change by the Fed in 2023 from a mostly open workspace to one with mostly closed office space caused a significant delay in the project's design. It also delayed the Fed from seeking a maximum cost ceiling for the project at that time.
The Fed has long blamed a range of factors for the cost overruns, including a spike in inflation that occurred as the economy emerged from the COVID-19 pandemic, unexpected expenses such as asbestos remediation, and additional demands from review agencies. For example, Trump appointees to a planning commission from his first term pushed the Fed to add more marble to the exterior of the renovated buildings, in keeping with Trump's preference for classical architecture.
The report said those factors all played a role, but added that they "do not account for the effect of key project management and contract execution decisions" that effectively transformed the contract to "a cost-plus reimbursement contract with a pay-as-you-go approach."
"Inflation does not change the Fed's responsibility to manage its resources prudently and be accountable to Congress," Sen. Tim Scott, chairman of the Senate Banking Committee and a South Carolina Republican, said.

For the first time since 2023, the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) on Sept. 16 raised interest rates by 25 basis points (bps). Fed funds futures had implied a greater than 50% probability of a hike since Chair Warsh’s August 28 Jackson Hole speech. With the economy and labor market resilient and inflation stubbornly above the Federal Reserve’s (Fed’s) 2% target, it decided to tighten policy.
What should investors take from this event? Considering today’s circumstances and looking back at the five times (1994, 1999, 2004, 2015 and 2022) the Fed has started a hiking cycle since the Fed began announcing policy decisions in 1994, and the one-off hike in 1997, we believe the following are worth considering:
Expect volatility. Across the six prior periods, the average maximum drawdown for the S&P 500 Index in the 12 months after the first hike was -12.2%, led by the -22.8% drawdown in 2022.
Look for opportunities. The average three-month return was -2.3%, and the average 12-month return was +8.7%. Given a backdrop of strong earnings growth and a strong economy, we think equity investors should use selloffs to rebalance and add diversified equity exposure.
Watch for higher yields. While on average, yields tend to rise in the lead-up to a Fed rate hike, the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield has also risen an average of 26.5 bps in the 12 months after. Given attractive starting yields today (unlike the low-rate environment in 2022), we think bonds are still attractive. We have favored shorter-duration bonds, but higher rates today and potentially higher rates ahead mean that core and core plus bond mandates are also becoming attractive.
The duration of the cycle will matter. We believe the economy and companies can stomach some increase in rates. If the Fed enters a prolonged hiking cycle and pushes rates to the point of breaking things, as occurred at the end of the hiking cycles that began in 1999, 2004, and 2022, then investors will need to remain more nimble. While unknowable at the time, the 1997 one-off hike was followed by a 12-month S&P 500 Index return of 39.8%.
What comes next for the Fed?
The FOMC has two meetings remaining this year; one is in the last week of October, which lands the week before the U.S. midterms, and the last one of the year takes place in the second week of December. The Summary of Economic Projections (SEP) indicates that participants expect one more rate hike in 2026. At the press conference, Chair Warsh provided little guidance on future policy, although his comments, coupled with the SEP, were viewed as hawkish by markets.

articles.title: Why Is Trump Ordering Fed Governor Lisa Cook To Face a White House Mortgage Fraud Hearing? - We Got This Covered
articles.summary: Why Is Trump Ordering Fed Governor Lisa Cook To Face a White House Mortgage Fraud Hearing?  We Got This Covered
articles.full_text:
President Donald Trump has ordered Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook to appear before a White House committee investigating allegations of mortgage fraud, taking his fight with the central bank into new territory.
According to the Associated Press, an executive memorandum issued on Oct. 9 established a “committee of inquiry” to investigate claims that Cook listed two different properties as her primary residence on mortgage applications in 2021. The allegations suggest she may have done so to secure lower interest rates.
Critics question the inquiry’s precedent
Trump has ordered Cook to attend a closed-door hearing at the White House on Nov. 5, 2026, where she will face questions about the applications. A full transcript is expected to be published after the hearing, although the public will not be able to follow the proceedings as they happen.
The move adds to months of legal wrangling over Trump’s attempts to remove Cook from the Federal Reserve’s seven-member Board of Governors. In June 2026, the Supreme Court blocked her summary removal but left open the possibility of the president pursuing it with proper notice and a hearing.
Trump has since appointed Kevin Hassett, Keith Sonderling, and Andrea Lucas to the inquiry panel. Former Federal Reserve Chief Counsel Scott Alvarez has argued that the move goes beyond earlier precedents, including a commission established under President William Howard Taft in 1912.
There is still the question of whether the allegations against Cook are enough to justify her removal. Federal law generally requires a president to show cause before dismissing a Fed governor, and legal experts have questioned whether a dispute over mortgage applications would meet that standard.
The timing of the inquiry is also difficult to ignore. Trump has repeatedly demanded interest rate cuts to stimulate the economy, while the Federal Reserve raised rates on Sept. 16, 2026, in a decision Cook supported despite pressure from the White House to do the opposite.
Wall Street analysts have viewed the proceedings as a possible way for Trump to replace Cook with someone more aligned with his economic priorities. The administration’s motives remain contested, however, and the mortgage allegations have yet to be resolved.
Civil rights advocates have raised concerns
Cook’s position on the board has brought another dimension to the dispute. She is the first Black woman to serve as a Federal Reserve governor, and civil rights advocates have raised concerns about the administration’s treatment of other prominent Black officials.
Her legal team is now weighing whether she will participate in the hearing as it considers how best to respond to the allegations. For Cook, the immediate issue is clearing her name. For the administration, the inquiry could become a route toward removing a governor who has resisted its pressure on interest rates.

articles.title: Goldman US Dollar To Yen Forecast: USD/JPY Tipped At 150 In 12 Months - Exchange Rates UK
articles.summary: Goldman US Dollar To Yen Forecast: USD/JPY Tipped At 150 In 12 Months  Exchange Rates UK
articles.full_text:
Analysts expect the Yen to strengthen against the US Dollar, but Japanese investors' continued overseas buying challenges the pace of recovery.
Japanese investors are still buying foreign assets heavily, testing Goldman Sachs' expectation that a shift in domestic policy will help the Yen recover against the US Dollar over the next year.
Goldman's latest forecasts put USD/JPY at 158 in three months, around January 2027, and 150 in 12 months, around October 2027.
The pair ended Friday near 158.33, leaving its near-term projection close to the market while the longer forecast requires a meaningful Yen appreciation.
An 8 October study of Japanese portfolio flows shows why that recovery may take time: investors with unhedged overseas holdings have yet to change direction decisively, even as banks sell foreign bonds.
Goldman's Karen Reichgott Fishman and colleagues say: "We recently turned structurally bullish Yen as the domestic policies that have weighed on the currency for much of the past 10-15 years appear to be shifting in a more supportive direction. The BoJ has seemingly shifted to a faster pace of hikes and, most importantly, there appears to be a focus within the government on encouraging some reallocation by domestic investors back towards domestic assets."
The latest evidence tests the shift behind Goldman's September reduction in its 12-month Dollar-Yen forecast from 165 to 150.
Higher Japanese rates can improve the return available at home, but a stronger domestic investment proposition still has to persuade savers to change what they buy.
Overseas equity buying remains strong
The Goldman analysts say: "We have been of the view that any shift in flows would likely be a slower-moving process, and so far that looks true among mostly unhedged investors."
Their reading of the Finance Ministry's September securities transactions release shows investment trusts, including retail investors and NISA savings-account flows, buying a net $8.7 billion of foreign equities, slightly more than in August.
NISA is Japan's tax-advantaged investment-account system.
MUFG's 9 October assessment reinforces that concern over a longer window.
Derek Halpenny, MUFG's head of research for global markets EMEA and international securities, says: "The buying has picked up and the 3mth sum of foreign equity purchases totalled JPY 3,949bn, a new record over a 3mth period."
Halpenny adds: "This Investment Trust flow captures households buying of foreign securities via NISA accounts and it remains clear that the expanded NISA limits adopted in January 2024 continues to have a notable impact."
Purchases of overseas investments without currency hedges create exposure to foreign currencies, potentially sustaining demand for them even as Japan's interest rates rise.
There is some moderation elsewhere, but slower buying is still different from bringing money home.
Goldman says: "The trust accounts category, which includes the public pension fund, suggests that net purchases of foreign bonds continued in September, but at a slower pace than in August ($7.6bn vs $14.7bn in August) and below the average pace of the prior six months ($8.6bn)."
"More broadly, our preferred estimate of key unhedged investor flows suggests that demand for foreign assets has generally persisted at a similar pace over the past year and shows no obvious signs of rotation. If that were to change, however, these data would be the first place to see it."
Bond sales do not tell the whole currency story
Japanese banks' foreign-bond sales accelerated to $15.9 billion in September, according to Goldman, while life insurers also remained net sellers.
Those sales could look like evidence supporting Goldman's recovery forecast, but currency hedges change their significance.
Goldman says: "While less relevant for the Yen, repatriation flows have been evident in the data for typically hedged investors (mainly banks and roughly 40% of flows by Lifers)."
A currency hedge already offsets some or all of an overseas holding's exchange-rate exposure, so selling the asset and unwinding that protection need not generate equivalent fresh demand for Yen.
The question is whether domestic policy can alter the choices of investors who have bought abroad without protection.
MUFG points to discussions about allowing Japanese government bonds within NISA accounts, following Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama's July suggestion that their inclusion should be considered.
That remains a potential policy change, rather than an implemented incentive already redirecting savings.
Halpenny says: "Providing tax-free opportunities to hold JGBs could well have an impact on the flows to foreign equity markets that is so evident today and given the scale of foreign equity purchases currently would be viewed as a clear yen positive."
