Summary
- PBOC CNY reference rate setting for the trading session ahead.
The People’s Bank of China publishes its daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time the previous evening), and the number has become one of the most closely followed signals in Asian currency markets. Its importance has grown over the past month as Beijing has moved from holding back the yuan’s rise to steering it gradually higher.
---
Earlier:
---
Under China’s managed float, the onshore yuan may trade up to 2% either side of the midpoint set each morning. The central bank arrives at that midpoint by weighing the previous session’s close, moves in the US dollar and other major currencies, wider global FX conditions, and domestic priorities including capital flows, growth and financial stability. Because the calculation leaves room for judgement, the fixing doubles as a tool for shaping expectations.
Once the rate is published, onshore trading proceeds within the band. If pressure drives the yuan toward either limit, the PBOC can respond by buying or selling the currency directly, adjusting liquidity, or acting through state-owned banks. That is why markets treat the fixing as a statement of intent. A midpoint stronger than forecast usually signals resistance to depreciation, while a weaker one can point to acceptance of a softer yuan, or discomfort with how quickly it is gaining.
For close to a year, the second message prevailed. The PBOC consistently set the midpoint weaker than market forecasts, which traders took as an effort to slow appreciation. That gap was at its widest since February in late August, soon after the yuan hit a three-and-a-half-year high against the dollar.
September marked a turning point. The central bank lifted the fixing for eight sessions in a row, its longest run since 2023, taking the midpoint to its strongest since February 2023. The onshore yuan climbed to levels last seen in January 2023 and the offshore rate to its firmest since July 2022. Yet the fixing is still being set well below estimates, at one point by more than 500 pips against a Reuters survey, suggesting Beijing is easing the brakes rather than releasing them.
Goldman Sachs analysts tied the firmer fixings to the run-up to the recent Trump-Xi summit, a pattern they said matches past diplomacy, and expect policymakers to remain comfortable with steady, gradual gains.
The trade-off has not changed. A stronger yuan supports capital stability and lowers import costs, but rapid gains could hurt exporters while the domestic economy remains soft. The daily gap between the fixing and consensus forecasts remains the clearest guide to how far Beijing will let the yuan run, and whether that tolerance outlasts the summit

articles.title: Rising Influence of Dollar and Euro in Cuba's Informal Market as Day Ends - CubaHeadlines
articles.summary: Rising Influence of Dollar and Euro in Cuba's Informal Market as Day Ends  CubaHeadlines
articles.full_text:
As of 8:00 PM local time in Cuba, the informal currency market wrapped up this Sunday, October 11, 2026, with the U.S. dollar and euro gaining ground compared to the previous day. The Cuban peso shows no signs of recovery, while foreign currencies remain at high levels. The MLC (freely convertible currency), with limited data available, offers only a rough guideline.
At the close of this Sunday, the U.S. dollar was valued at 785 Cuban pesos (CUP), reflecting an increase of 2.5 pesos from the previous day when the average rate was 783 CUP. On a weekly basis, the dollar stayed steady at 785 CUP, the same level as seven days ago. Over the past month, the U.S. dollar has surged by 93.5 pesos from 692 CUP, marking a 13.5% rise, although it's important to note that part of this change may be due to methodological adjustments in the index. The dollar continues to set the pace in the informal market amidst a structural shortage of foreign currencies.
The euro concluded the day at 878 Cuban pesos (CUP), marking a rise of 2 pesos from the previous day's close of 876 CUP. In a weekly comparison, the euro dipped marginally by 1 peso from 879 CUP a week ago, a nearly negligible change. Compared to 30 days ago, the euro has gained 93 pesos, an increase of 11.9%. However, this figure should be considered with the same caution as the dollar regarding potential methodological adjustments. It stands as the most expensive currency in the Cuban parallel market, surpassing the dollar by 93 pesos.
MLC and Its Limited Influence
The MLC closed around 535 Cuban pesos (CUP), though this value should be regarded as merely indicative due to the scarcity of available data at this time. Compared to the previous day, it showed an increase of 38 pesos, and on a weekly basis, it climbed 3 pesos from 532 CUP a week ago. Without physical existence, its usage is limited to state-run stores that accept it, restricting its circulation compared to cash currencies.
Exchange Rate Discrepancies
Exchange rates as of Sunday, October 11, 2026, are as follows: 1 USD equals 785 CUP, 1 EUR equals 878 CUP, and MLC stands at an indicative 535 CUP with limited data. The official exchange rate from the Central Bank of Cuba (Segment III) remains significantly lower, at 698 CUP per dollar and 781 CUP per euro, compared to the prevailing rates in the informal market. The gap between the official and informal dollar rates exceeds 87 pesos, while for the euro, the difference is nearly 97 pesos.
Although Segment III was introduced as a more flexible exchange mechanism, its official rates remain far from aligning with the informal market, failing to meet the real currency demand of the population. Over the past month, the official dollar rate increased from 651 to 698 CUP, and the euro from 757 to 781 CUP, highlighting the ongoing pressure on the Cuban peso, even in the institutional channel.
Impact on Cuban Economy
In a scenario marked by sustained inflation, low state salaries, and increasing partial dollarization of the economy, each fluctuation in the informal market directly affects internal prices and Cubans' purchasing power. The close of this Sunday reaffirms that foreign currencies remain robust against a peso struggling to find stability.
The informal currency market in Cuba operates outside state financial institutions, through networks of private buying and selling. Although not officially recognized by the Cuban regime, it effectively determines the real purchasing power of Cubans.
The CiberCuba Exchange Rate is an index of the Cuban informal market, created from the automated analysis of thousands of currency trade posts in Telegram and Facebook groups. The calculation filters out atypical offers and spam, weighing each transaction by its recency to consolidate a representative value that updates several times a day.
Understanding Cuba's Informal Currency Market
Why are foreign currencies gaining ground in Cuba's informal market?
Foreign currencies like the U.S. dollar and euro are gaining ground due to the Cuban peso's continued weakness and the structural shortage of foreign exchange in the country.
How does the official exchange rate compare to the informal market rate?
The official exchange rate is significantly lower than the informal market rate. For example, the official rate for the dollar is 698 CUP, while the informal market rate is 785 CUP, creating a gap of over 87 pesos.

articles.summary: Trump's quest to bring down gas prices ahead of the midterms is not going great  Business InsiderFor the first time ever, 10-year bond yields track diesel prices more closely than crude, and Trump’s fuel deal with Putin may be too little too late  Yahoo FinanceTrump to push US officials to use Defense Production Act to raise oil, fuel output, three sources say  ReutersTrump wants to reduce the cost of fuel as the midterms loom - will it work?  BBCAnalysis ...
articles.full_text:
President Donald Trump is running into the limits of his influence as he seeks to bring down sky-high gas prices ahead of the midterm elections.
In social media posts and stump speeches across the country, Trump has sought to assure voters that gas prices — a major sticking point for Americans grappling with an affordability crisis — will soon go down.
At the White House on Friday, for instance, Trump recalled seeing gas prices below $2 a gallon in Iowa before the US and Israel launched surprise strikes on Iran in February.
"We'll be down to those levels soon," he said.
The numbers and the trajectory of conflicts around the world, however, portend a different story.
As of Sunday, AAA reported that the average price of regular gas in the US was $4.36 per gallon. At this time last year, that number was $3.09. Diesel prices have also skyrocketed, reaching $6.28 per gallon earlier this month.
Early Monday, Brent crude, the international oil benchmark, was trading about 2% lower at around $103 a barrel.
That's more than 40% above its level at the start of the Iran war, but about 2% below where it stood a month ago, after prices surged past $100 a barrel in early September.
The bigger concern, however, is diesel, where prices have remained elevated despite crude's recent pullback.
Refinery bottlenecks and attacks on energy infrastructure in the Middle East and Russia have squeezed supplies of the fuel, which powers trucks, trains, ships, and farm equipment. That raises transportation costs across the economy and can keep inflation under pressure even if crude prices stabilize.
Persistently high diesel prices also pose a political challenge ahead of the midterms, as rising transportation costs threaten to add to the inflation pressures already weighing on American households.
Trump suspended fuel export sanctions on Russia this week to bring more diesel to the market and lower prices, prompting allies and enemies alike to wrinkle an eyebrow. Hours later, Ukraine struck a Russian oil depot.
On Sunday morning, Trump tried again to calm oil markets, announcing an "ENERGY CEASEFIRE" between Russia and Ukraine on Truth Social.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on X, however, that while he supports such a ceasefire, the deal was news to him. He added that a Russian drone struck a power plant in Kyiv on Sunday.
Meanwhile, on Saturday in the Strait of Hormuz, through which oil shipments have slowed to a trickle as Iran flexes its control of the key waterway — a big reason the price of oil has increased and gas prices have spiked — an oil tanker struck a mine and caught on fire.
The US-Israeli war on Iran is only expanding as Iranian allies target Saudi Arabia, a US ally, and its oil infrastructure. Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen have expanded their control of the coast bordering the Red Sea and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a key shipping lane for Saudi oil exports. And last month, the group orchestrated an attack from southeastern Iraq on a major Saudi oil pipeline, forcing Saudi Arabia to temporarily shut it down.
An attack on King Khalid International Airport by Houthi fighters on Saturday killed 12 people and injured over 300. One American was killed, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said, and officials were forced to briefly close the airport.
At this rate, it's hard to imagine oil prices softening enough to relieve Americans of high gas prices by the time they head to the polls in November.

articles.summary: Is 8% next? Why mortgage rates have surged, and may stay higher for longer  Yahoo FinanceThe 'Oracle of Wall Street' says prepare for a prolonged housing slowdown as rates and home prices refuse to budge  Business InsiderHow 7.4% Mortgages Are Giving Buyers Leverage in a Stuck Housing Market  WSJHome Sales: "High" Interest Rates Are Not the Problem. High Prices Are.  Mises InstituteToday’s Mortgage Rates, October 11: 5/1 ARM Falls 12 Basis Points as Fixed ...
articles.full_text:
Mortgage rates are on a rough ride. In just over a month, they're up a full percentage point to around 7.5%, a three-year high. Buyers are pulling back in response, and September home sales look poised for a steep downturn.
How did this happen? Blame surging bond yields worldwide. Mortgage rates are particularly sensitive to the movements of the 10-year Treasury yield (^TNX), which has jumped to multiyear highs in recent weeks.
Read more: How to get the lowest mortgage rates right now
Unpacking what's moving bond yields higher so quickly is more complicated. Economists point to a web of factors causing investors to rewrite their expectations for inflation and economic growth.
"There's clearly a trend," said Daryl Fairweather, chief economist at Redfin. "There's something meaningful happening with us moving into a higher-for-longer economy."
While it's impossible to predict where bond yields and mortgage rates go from here, 8% loans now look like a not-so-distant possibility. Here's why experts told Yahoo Finance the current environment looks like one where rates could stay high, and even keep rising.
Oil prices and Iran
Mortgage rates jolted higher in the weeks after the US attacked Iran on Feb. 28 as investors fretted about rising oil prices and their implications for inflation. Although oil prices have fallen from their peaks, concern remains about how higher energy prices will reverberate across supply chains, potentially worsening inflation.
Apart from oil prices themselves, general uncertainty about the situation in Iran is also pushing rates higher, as investors want more compensation for unknown risks, said Jake Krimmel, senior economist at Realtor.com.
"The geopolitical uncertainty is a huge part of it," Krimmel said. "We're talking about supply shock. That doesn't just touch oil, but probably everything else with trade."
Meanwhile, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who has tried to lower bond yields via buybacks to little effect, has blamed much of the rise in bond yields and mortgage rates on energy prices.
"I don't know if this conflict's going to end next week, next month, in two months, but I believe on the other side of this, energy prices will be much lower and interest rates, mortgage rates will come back down," he said on Monday.
Read more: How soaring Treasury yields could hit your finances
Economic growth
Still, few economists think energy prices alone explain today's higher rates, because the US economy has been showing the kind of growth that typically causes bond yields and mortgage rates to rise.

articles.summary: Musk vows ‘affordable’ Starlink in India as he escalates feud with Ambani  Al JazeeraMusk vows affordable Starlink in India days before Ambani's record Jio IPO  ReutersStarlink faces affordability test in India as low-cost telecom plans dominate market  Telegraph IndiaIndia’s security policy not shaped by social media pressure, says Nishikant Dubey amid Starlink row  The HinduNo special treatment for American firms as US-India ties sour  Business...
articles.full_text:
Billionaire entrepreneur Elon Musk has said he would price his Starlink satellite internet service affordably in India to take on Mukesh Ambani’s low-cost Reliance Jio, escalating his attacks on the rival tycoon days before Jio’s parent launches the country’s largest-ever initial public offering (IPO).
Jio Platforms, which owns the telecom arm, is targeting a valuation of $106bn in the offering. Much like SpaceX-owned Starlink, Jio’s satellite venture is also awaiting final security clearance to launch.
Cheap data is the playbook that built Jio in India, and the one Musk has used in markets like Kenya to unsettle local telecom players. SpaceX now plans to enter the mobile carrier market itself, starting in the United States.
Musk did not specify prices for India, where mobile data costs about rupees 7.74 ($0.08) per gigabyte, among the lowest in the world.
“Obviously, if Starlink is too expensive in India, no one will buy it, so SpaceX will need to make pricing affordable,” he said in a post on his social media platform X on Saturday.
“The reality is that competition would greatly benefit the average citizen in India by giving them more choices, as it always does. Ambani’s profits will be lower, but he is not going out of business,” Musk added.
‘Prime Minister Ambani’
Musk’s remarks were the latest in a series of X posts in which he accused Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government and Ambani of stalling Starlink’s entry into one of the world’s biggest internet markets to favour market leader Jio.
The posts have marked a sharp turn for Musk, who has long enjoyed a warm public rapport with Modi.
India’s government has denied any bias in its approval process, noting that the three satellite ventures seeking to launch, including Starlink’s and Jio’s, are all awaiting final security clearance.
Late on Friday, Musk taunted Ambani directly, addressing him as “Prime Minister Ambani” and asking whether he would “consider allowing Starlink to compete”.
Reliance has not responded to Musk’s remarks.

articles.title: ‘Some aren’t going to make it’: how pressure on farmers threatens UK food security
articles.summary: Food producers are adding their voices to the chorus of warnings about the vulnerability of British supply chains“There are so many decent, capable, productive, efficient arable farmers out there, asking how they are supposed to finance the crop they are meant to be putting in the ground,” Jamie Burrows says.Sitting in his tractor at his arable farm in Norfolk, Burrows is listing the multiple challenges facing him and other food producers. articles.full_text:
“There are so many decent, capable, productive, efficient arable farmers out there, asking how they are supposed to finance the crop they are meant to be putting in the ground,” Jamie Burrows says.
Sitting in his tractor at his arable farm in Norfolk, Burrows is listing the multiple challenges facing him and other food producers.
Crop growers such as Burrows are ploughing and cultivating their fields, preparing the ground – hardened and dried out during the long, hot summer – for their next crop.
But machinery requires fuel, and the cost of red diesel – used for agricultural vehicles and machinery that is taxed at a lower rate than standard diesel – has almost doubled since the conflict in Iran began in late February. The cost of most fertilisers used to grow crops and feed for animals has also soared by about 20% over the same period.
“Some of these businesses aren’t going to make it,” concludes Burrows, who is also the chair of the crops board at the National Farmers’ Union (NFU). “It is very, very difficult.”
These are among the latest worries for Britain’s food producers, who also faced a succession of heatwaves and drought conditions during the UK’s hottest summer on record, which resulted in England’s worst recorded cereals harvest, according to official production estimates.
Farmers, the first link in the food production chain, are adding their voices to the chorus of warnings about the vulnerability and precarity of the UK’s food supply.
Food experts, academics, businesses and the public spending watchdog, the National Audit Office (NAO), have in recent weeks called on the government to work on making the UK’s food system more resilient.
The climate crisis, this year’s huge El Niño weather pattern, geopolitical shocks, energy outages and cyber-attacks are all considered threats to food chain security.
Amid calls for ministers to treat food as a national security issue, parliament’s influential public accounts committee is to begin a series of hearings on Monday as part of its inquiry into the resilience of the UK’s food supply.
MPs on the committee will look at the NAO’s findings on the shortcomings of the last catastrophe planning exercise by the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra), which largely excluded food supply chain businesses.
Britain produces about 60% of the food it needs to feed itself, but is more dependent on imports than many European peers. The government’s own research has shown Britons are less prepared for potential future emergencies than several European neighbours.
Some in the food industry believe there are signs Andy Burnham’s government is beginning to take the threats to Britain’s food system more seriously.
The Cabinet Office will launch a campaign telling households to stock up on tinned foods alongside preparations for possible future emergencies. The government’s Prepare website outlines steps it says people should take, which include storing items at home, including bottles of water and nonperishable food, such as tinned meat, fruit and vegetables that do not require cooking.
Despite this, a recent warning from more than 150 food experts and academics accused ministers of being “complacent” about food security and not having a plan to feed people in an emergency.
“Historically we have done pretty well coping with specific events such as Covid and we’ve managed to ride through them, but we’re moving into a period where we’re having multiple crises impact at the same time,” says Prof Paul Behrens of the Oxford Martin School, University of Oxford, who signed the letter.
These include the worsening climate crisis and increased water scarcity in regions that now provide some of the fresh produce UK households rely on, including the Mediterranean and north Africa.
Meanwhile, Behrens and other experts, including Prof Tim Lang of the Centre for Food Policy, City St George’s, University of London, have been warning for some time that the UK’s food distribution network is concentrated, leaving it exposed to potential disruption or targeting by bad actors.
Lang has previously stated that the UK’s supermarket network is supplied by just 131 distribution hubs – serving 12,300 stores – while the industry body the Cold Chain Federation has warned that most of Britain’s food imports enter the country through four ports – Dover, Felixstowe, Southampton and London Gateway.
The UK government wound up the strategic food stockpile that had been in place since the second world war in the 1990s. Behrens says other nations, particularly Scandinavian countries, now have “far greater national preparedness”.
He says: “They’re looking at community responses and how much households can have on hand. They’re looking at their own local production and some countries have strategic stores of grain.”
Mother of one Ana, 42, is one of a small but growing number of citizens who have been preparing for possible future emergencies for some time. Now living in south Wales, she is originally from eastern Europe and grew up in a family that grew food and preserved it for the colder months. She now shares tips on her YouTube channel, advising other households on resilience and how to build an emergency stockpile.
“It’s just a normal way of life, basically safeguarding yourself and your family,” she says. Ana describes herself as a “prepper”, but wants to move away from its negative connotations, such as panic buying or being a survivalist.
“The stereotype was … that preparedness is American, really weird, all camo and blokes in the bushes, hunting and eating squirrels and mushrooms,” she says. Instead she wants to help other citizens learn how they could cope for a few hours, days or even weeks without power, water or being able to get to the shops.
“If the stereotype had been dispersed originally by the government, then people would look at preparedness as an everyday thing,” she says.
Rob Haward, the chief executive of organic vegetable box delivery company Riverford, believes the UK’s food supply chain needs a “very complicated rethink and a different vision for future security”.
Devon-based Riverford distributes about 65,000 boxes a week to customers and about 70% of the produce it sells is grown in the UK, although it also has long-term relationships with growers in Spain and Italy.
While the UK is always going to import fruit such as bananas, which cannot be grown in large volumes domestically, Haward believes consumers can also play a role by returning to eating more seasonally.
Haward says longer-term contracts can help farmers, giving them confidence to invest in their land and what they grow. He adds: “There are different ways we can try to create a food and farming sector different to now and much more resilient to the future world,” such as working to restore soils to better withstand the changing climate. He also wants government to “pull levers” such as offering lower business rates to greengrocers.
